title.en: Suguid and the Hidden Princess: The Musical Purlon
title.zh: 蘇吉德與隱居公主：奏樂的寶匣

region.en: Angeles, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省安赫勒斯（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Pampangan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 21 'Is he the Crafty Ulysses?', eBook #8299

summary.en: Abandoned by his parents for eating the house, the foundling Suguid outgrows his school in five months and, by mysterious combinations of characters on paper, discovers that the king has a hidden daughter — posting the fact on the palace door at the price of his head. Twelve goldsmiths build him the purlon, a five-foot jewel-box that plays the sweetest music mortal ears had ever heard; the charmed king borrows it for a night, Suguid steps out poniard in hand, wins the princess's ring by passionate speech, and is married to her when the wager is paid.
summary.zh: 因食量驚人而被父母遺棄的孤兒蘇吉德，五個月便學盡書堂；他以紙上神算推知國王藏有公主，竟在王宮門上貼出此事，以頭顱為注。十二名金匠為他打造『寶匣』——奏出凡人未曾聽過的仙樂。著迷的國王借匣一晚；蘇吉德持匕首現身，以深情言辭贏得公主戒指；賭約到期，二人成婚。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan folktale recorded by Fansler from a Licup narrator (Angeles); archival record. Bride-wager type (golden musical carriage); Fansler compares the Tagalog corrido 'Juan Bachiller' and southern-European variants.

passages.text: Balbino and Alaga had only one child, a son named Suguid, who was at first greatly beloved by them; the couple was very rich. But the son was a voracious eater: while still a baby he used to pull up the nails from the floor and eat them when his mother had no more milk to give him, and when all the nails were exhausted he ate the cotton with which the pillows were stuffed — his parents compared him to a mill which consumes sugarcane incessantly. Before many years the wealth of the couple had been greatly diminished by the lavish expenditure they had to make for Suguid's food; at last they decided to cast him away into a place from which he might not be able to find his way home again, and led him one day to a dense forest and abandoned him there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 21 'Is he the Crafty Ulysses?'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Luckily a merchant passed by, found the crying boy, took him home, and put him in school; in a few weeks the boy showed his superiority over his classmates, in time beat even the master in points of learning, and after only five months of studying he left the school because he found it too small for his expanding intellect. By some mathematical calculation, so the tradition says, or by certain mysterious combinations of characters that he wrote on paper, Suguid discovered one day that a certain princess was hidden somewhere, concealed so that her existence might not be known other than by her parents and the courtiers. He went to the palace of the king and posted a paper on the palace-door: 'Your Majesty cannot deny me the fact that he has a daughter secluded somewhere. Your humble servant, Suguid Bociu.' The king, now unable to keep the secret of his daughter's existence, summoned him: 'Very well — if you can prove what you have stated, I will give you my daughter for your bride. If within three days you fail to produce her before me, however, you shall be unconditionally executed.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 21 'Is he the Crafty Ulysses?'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Oh, do not be afraid, father! If you will but provide me with twelve of the best goldsmiths that can be found in the whole city, I have no doubt of finding and captivating the fair princess.' The merchant summoned all the good goldsmiths, and Suguid ordered them to make a purlon of gold, silver, and precious stones — oblong in shape, hollow inside, five feet high, three feet deep, and four feet long, with a chair and a lamp inside, and by a certain device a person inside could breathe; altogether its construction was so beautiful that it seemed as if it were intended for the sight of the gods alone. Suguid entered it with provisions, fine clothes, a poniard, and a guitar, and ordered five men to carry it toward the king's palace while he played the sweetest piece of music mortal ears had ever heard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 21 'Is he the Crafty Ulysses?'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Near the palace the king, charmed by the melodious music, asked that the purlon be lent him: 'Oh, how happy our daughter would be if she should hear this enchanting piece of music! If you will lend me this purlon, you may ask of me as a compensation any favor that you may want.' The princess was so bewitched by the music that she told her father never to take it away from her; and when the king and queen had gone, Suguid listened carefully to their retreating footsteps, came out poniard in hand, and knelt: 'Fair princess, let not my presence cause any fear!... Your ring, my adored princess, will give me life or death — life, because I shall be spared from being beheaded; death, for I have promised your father to present your ring to him within three days as a token of your acceptance of my suit. Therefore, Queen of Beauty, choose: your ring, or my death. I have my poniard ready, and I prefer a hundred times to die — nay, die smiling — at your hands.' Moved by this passionate speech, after a difficult struggle within herself she gave him the ring; Suguid entered the purlon again, was returned to the agent in the morning, and on the appointed day appeared at the palace carrying the emblem of his victory. The king knew that he was lost, and he swooned; on recovering he reluctantly caused the princess to be summoned, and she and Suguid were married — and by Suguid's wise policy the kingdom prospered, and for the first time learned what peace really meant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 21 'Is he the Crafty Ulysses?'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Reward of Kindness: The Devil's Seven-Year Wager
title.zh: 善行的報償：魔鬼的七年之賭

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 22 'The Reward of Kindness', eBook #8299

summary.en: Childless Clara vows 'I would even let my son serve the Devil'; nine years later a bear-like visitor claims her Idó. The Devil exchanges clothes with the youth, gives him a bag of money, and frees him if he spends seven years' wandering doing good — or hell if he squanders it. In bear-skin he ransoms a poor old woman from prison, marries her youngest daughter who alone will have him, and returns at the seven years' end to swap suits with the Devil; the two sisters who mocked the bear nearly die of vexation when the knight arrives with the half-ring token.
summary.zh: 無子的克拉拉曾許願『寧讓兒子侍奉魔鬼』；九年後熊形惡魔登門索子。魔鬼與少年換衣、給其一袋金錢，訂約：七載行善則釋，揮霍則墮地獄。熊皮少年替老嫗還債免獄，老嫗以三女許婚，唯幼女應允。七年期滿，他與魔鬼換回騎士裝束，持半枚戒指登門——譏笑過熊的兩位姊姊幾乎氣死。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Cordero narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. Fansler notes it as a Bear-Skin (Grimm No. 101) import, the only Orient-recorded version, with a native promised-child opening and a broken-ring recognition unique in Filipino tales.

passages.text: In a certain town there once lived a couple who had never had a child, though married nearly five years and very anxious for a son — Clara the wife, Philip the man. One cloudy night in December, while they were talking by the window of their house, Clara said to her husband that she was going to pray the novena so that Heaven would give them a child: 'I would even let my son serve the Devil, if he would but give us a son!' Her husband was willing that she should pray the novena, and Clara began the next day her fervent devotions to the Virgin Mary, going to church every afternoon for nine days. At last she finished her novenario — but no child was born to them, and the couple was disappointed. A month had passed when, to their great happiness, Clara gave birth to a son, whom they nicknamed Idó.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 22 'The Reward of Kindness'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Idó was greatly cherished by his parents, but did not care much to stay at home: he early began to show a fondness for travelling abroad, and was always to be found in the dense woods on the outskirts of the town. One afternoon, when the family was gathered around a small table, a knock was heard at the door, and Clara, trembling, opened it to see standing there a man who looked like a bear. 'A devil, a devil!' she exclaimed; but the Devil pacified her: 'Clara, I have come here to get your son you promised me a long time ago. Now that the day has come when your son can be of some service to me, will you deny your promise?' Clara called her son: 'Here is my son. Take him, since he is yours.' Idó, about seventeen years old, was not frightened by the Devil, and finally consented to go, because of his mother's promise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 22 'The Reward of Kindness'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Devil took Idó to his cave far away outside the town, and tried in many ways to tempt him but was unable, because Idó was a youth of strong character; finally the Devil decided to exchange clothes with him. Idó was obliged to put on the bear-like clothes of the Devil and to give him his own soldier-suit; then the Devil produced a large bag full of money: 'Take this money and go travelling about the world for seven years. If you live to the end of that time, and spend this money only in doing good, I will set you free. If, however, you spend the money extravagantly, you will have to go to hell with me.' And he disappeared. Idó began his wanderings from town to town; whenever people saw him they were afraid of him and would refuse him shelter, but Idó would give them money from his bag, and then they would gather about him and be kind to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 22 'The Reward of Kindness'; not verbatim.

passages.text: After many years he came to a town where he saw an old woman summoned before a court of justice, accused of owing a sum of money she was unable to pay; when Idó paid her fine for her and thus released her from prison, she could hardly express her gratitude, and as most of the other people were afraid of Idó, this woman decided to take him home with her. She had three daughters, and called her eldest: 'Here is a man who delivered me from prison. As I can do nothing to reward him for his great kindness, I want you to take him for your husband.' 'Mother, why have you brought this ugly man here? No, I cannot marry him'; the second daughter refused just as her sister had, and made fun of the man. Finally the youngest daughter said, 'Mother, if to have me marry this man is the only way by which you can repay him for his kindness, I'll gladly marry him.' A contract was signed between them, but before they were married the bear-like man asked permission to be absent one more year to finish his duty; she consented, and gave him half her ring as a memento.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 22 'The Reward of Kindness'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the end of the year, which was the last of his seven years' wandering, the bear-like man went to the Devil and told him that he had finished his duty. 'You have beaten me. Now that you have performed your seven years' wandering, and have spent the money honestly, let us exchange clothes again!' So the man received back his soldierlike suit, which made him look like a knight, and the Devil took back his bear-skin. Then the man returned to Clara's house; when his arrival was announced, the two older daughters dressed themselves in their best, thinking he was a suitor come to see them — but when the man showed the ring and asked for the hand of Clara's youngest daughter, the two nearly died with vexation, while the youngest daughter was very happy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 22 'The Reward of Kindness'; not verbatim.

title.en: Pedro and Satan: The Cross-Embroidered Gowns
title.zh: 佩德羅與撒旦：繡十字的長袍

region.zh: 菲律賓卡坦端內斯島（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Bicol oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 23 'Pedro and Satan', eBook #8299

summary.en: A childless rich man sells himself and his wife to Satan for a son; born full-grown in five days, Pedro learns his fate and refuses to marry until he has wrested the golden document from hell. Armed with gowns hung with little crosses, he frightens hauling demons into flight by lifting his robe at each 'One, two, three!', ties the napping Satan to his own rocking-chair, and burns the bond before freeing the terrified fiend — saving his parents and his future child from a terrible fate.
summary.zh: 無子的富翁以己及妻獻給撒旦換取子嗣；五日即成的佩德羅得知契約，誓不婚娶，定要從地獄奪回金契。他身披綴滿小十字架的長袍下獄：每喊『一、二、三』便掀袍示十字，拖木的群魔抱頭鼠竄；他再把打盹的撒旦綁在搖椅上，火燒金契，方才鬆手——嚇破膽的魔王一逃了之。

sensitivity.note: Bicol folktale recorded by Fansler from a Sorreta narrator (Catanduanes); archival record. Promised-Child cycle; Fansler compares Lorraine, Wallachian, and Lithuanian variants.

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived a very rich man whose wife had never given birth to a child; the couple had made several pilgrimages and spent great sums of money for religious services in the hope that God might give them a child, even though a sickly one, to inherit their money — but all their efforts were in vain. Disappointed, the man resolved to rely upon Satan for the performance of his wish. One dark night, when he was thinking hard about the matter, he heard a voice say, 'Your wish will be quickly fulfilled if you but ask me for it.' Filled with joy, he turned towards the voice and knelt before the invisible speaker: 'I will give you my life, and even my wife's, in return for a son who will be the heir to my riches.' A figure in front of him assumed in an instant the form of Satan, and they made a golden document which provided that the first child of the heir was to be given to the Devil at the age of ten, and that the man and his wife were no longer God's subjects, but Satan's.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 23 'Pedro and Satan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The child was born at the appointed time and grew wonderfully fast, for in five days he was a full-grown youth; but the parents could not but blame themselves for their impious act. They intended to keep the secret from their son, but could not do so, for the boy was always asking about the nature of his existence. So when Pedro knew of his pitiful lot, he decided not to marry until he had succeeded in wresting the golden document from the hands of Satan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 23 'Pedro and Satan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Pedro knew that devils do not like crosses, and cannot even stay where they have to look at them; so one day he asked his mother to make for him two gowns, one having little crosses hanging from it. When these had been finished, Pedro asked his father to give him over to Satan, so that he might work with the demons in hell; no sooner had he expressed his desire than the Devil appeared and took the young man off to his kingdom, where Pedro was assigned the task of directing the demons in hauling the logs that were to be used for fuel. Pedro ordered the demons to tie a strong piece of rope to one end of a log and pull it while he stood on the other end; every time he counted 'One, two, three!' he would hold up his outer gown, and the demons, seeing the crosses, would run away in confusion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 23 'Pedro and Satan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: As the devils could not endure Pedro's conduct they ran to their master Satan, asking him to send the young man away, for he could not do any work — yet the demons could not say anything about Pedro's trick, for they did not dare even speak the word 'cross.' Satan then summoned Pedro to his office and had him work there. The young man had put a strong piece of rope under his gown: one day, when Satan was taking his siesta in a rocking-chair, Pedro tied him fast to the chair, removed his outer gown, and woke Satan. The Devil with closed eyes struggled hard to escape, but could not get loose; so he humbly requested Pedro to go away and leave him alone — but Pedro would neither leave him nor let him go. He demanded the document, and Satan would not give it up; so Pedro kept on frightening the Devil until at last Satan said he would give up the document if Pedro would release him. Pedro put on his outer robe, and the Devil called his secretary and told him to give the golden document to the young man; Pedro threw the bond into the fire, and when he saw that it was completely melted he took off his outer robe again and turned Satan loose. The Devil ran away exceedingly terrified. Then Pedro went home, where his parents received him with great joy: thus by his cleverness he saved his parents and his future child from a terrible fate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 23 'Pedro and Satan'; not verbatim.
